paragraphs.source_en: Around the animal there are anthropomorphic figures and a mask, identical to those in the previous shelter. Under the animal a male figure with body decoration and a bow has also been repainted. Here again, the area in front of the shelter is delimited by small stones put side by side in a regular line leading to the adjacent shelter which is without paintings but contains a big boulder with several kettles and cupules (see figure 2-2).

paragraphs.source_en: Contrary to the main shelters which are exposed to the large plain, the next small shelter is hidden inside the stone city. It is located just behind the shelter with the large down-headed animal but it is not visible from outside; the images were placed deliberately in a hidden corner of the site. It presents a row of four very simple small-sized figures, two larger and two smaller (Fig. 5-3). The bigger figures, a man and a woman, are followed by a couple, the reduced dimension of which may express their minor age, so that this might be a familiar scene of parents and children. The small figures are holding an enigmatic triangular object.

paragraphs.source_en: For its open character and visibility from a great distance it is unlikely that Tin Aboteka was a secret place but it may have served as a public place for possible meetings. The images of masks, decorated and dancing figures might testify to possible rituals that occurred directly in the site. The place must have been suitable for a large number of people even over a long period since the area is vast, water was available and the surrounding plain offered possibility for hunting.
